title: Antidepressants: long-term use and tapering
text:
This topic (antidepressant use longer term and tapering) is getting a lot of attention in the media (NYT, NPR, etc.) with a lot of confusion for the general public.  My goal here is to call out what is fringe and what is not adequately supported in current practice and is hype!

Depression is a very common disorder, and antidepressants are one of the most commonly prescribed medications in the US and have benefitted many people. The goal here is not to critique the science or the practice of psychiatry. Since Prozac was approved in 1988, there are many FDA approved agents. Unlike disorders such as hypertension where patients are on meds long term, we do not think of antidepressants as a lifelong therapy for most patients. In general, these agents are used for 3-6-12 months, combined with lifestyle changes and talk therapy. Thereafter, based on clinical improvement a decision is made to discontinue these agents, typically over a few weeks and patients do well.  

Sometimes, patients may remain on these agents much longer for a variety of reasons ranging from changing providers, lack of clarity as to response, situational factors, etc. This may extend to years or longer with failed attempts to successfully wean or stop the antidepressants. One obvious reason for failure to successfully stop these agents is relapse of the underlying disease. A second reason could be the method or rapidity of a weaning protocol. This is the context that is under much discussion.  A champion in this area is Dr. Horowitz, a psychiatrist from Australia, started a movement called Outro, that most taper failures occur not because the patient still needs the antidepressant but because of “the method.”  He proposed a "hyperbolic taper protocol" that posits that a much slower taper is required based on some mechanistic studies using PET scans (and serotonin receptor occupancy). 
This is the link to the Horowitz method (and their commercial site):

https://www.outro.com/

Horowitz et al. did not randomize patients to: ordinary tapering vs hyperbolic tapering, and demonstrate fewer clinically significant withdrawal symptoms, higher successful discontinuation rates or lower recurrence rates. They analyzed pharmacologic and PET data and proposed a regimen.
That makes hyperbolic tapering a mechanistically informed strategy, not a clinically proven optimum strategy.  This is a critically important point that is lost in the public reporting. There is a very loud and online active contingency, together with the MAHA crowd that is adding confusion and giving these agents a bad name.

Medicine has long recognized that physiological adaptation can require gradual withdrawal. But we generally do not derive extremely precise taper schedules solely from receptor occupancy curves, as Horowitz suggests. There are many examples including benzodiazepines, opioids, beta blockers, and corticosteroids where clinicians routinely wean.

Horowitz identified a genuine flaw in the old practice of simply halving antidepressants a few times and stopping them. His hyperbolic model offers an elegant pharmacologic explanation for why some patients struggle disproportionately at low doses, and it has appropriately influenced contemporary tapering guidance.

But the Outro brochure converts that useful insight into a much stronger clinical claim than the evidence presently supports.

The main weaknesses are:

treating SERT occupancy as a surrogate for withdrawal physiology;
extrapolating PET data into a precise tapering schedule without definitive randomized clinical validation;
presenting the controversial 56% withdrawal estimate as settled when substantially lower controlled estimates now exist;
minimizing genuine depression/anxiety recurrence as a cause of failed discontinuation;
implying that extremely low compounded doses are broadly necessary rather than valuable primarily for a selected withdrawal-sensitive subgroup; and
presenting a commercially provided method as essentially “what the science says.”

The pharmacology of other drug classes actually supports a moderate version of Horowitz rather than the strongest version: corticosteroids, benzodiazepines and opioids all demonstrate that chronic drug exposure can require slower reductions near the end and individualized tapering. But none justifies assuming that a receptor-occupancy curve alone specifies the clinically optimal withdrawal regimen.

So, I would characterize hyperbolic antidepressant tapering as a plausible and useful technique—particularly for long-term users with previous withdrawal—not as a demonstrated biological law of antidepressant discontinuation.

And the claim from Outro that “the reason most tapers fail isn't because you need the medication; it's because of the method” is, in my view, the sentence least defensible from the available evidence.
